73579.q: What is the soluble fibre in apples called, which is also used to set jam?
73579.e: Pectin is found in apples, quinces and citrus fruits. It binds water and makes jam set.

73580.q: What in the gut partly feeds on fibre?
73580.e: Much fibre is broken down in the large intestine by useful bacteria. It is food for healthy gut flora.
73580.m: Fibre is food for the gut bacteria.

73581.q: What is the insoluble fibre called that plant cell walls are mainly made of?
73581.e: Cellulose is the main part of plant cell walls. Humans cannot digest it, but it keeps the gut active.
73581.m: Plant cell walls are mainly made of cellulose.

73582.q: Why do growing children and teenagers need more energy per kilogram of body weight than adults?
a: The body needs energy to grow
73582.e: While growing, the body builds new bones, muscles and other tissues. For this it needs extra energy and enough nutrients.

73583.q: What does the energy density of a food tell you?
a: How much energy is in a certain amount
73583.e: Energy density says how many kilocalories or kilojoules a food provides per gram or per 100 grams. Vegetables have a low energy density, nuts and chocolate a high one.
73583.m: Energy density shows how much energy is in one gram of food.

73584.q: What is the energy called that the body needs at complete rest for breathing, heartbeat and body warmth?
73584.e: The basal metabolic rate is the energy needed at rest. When you move, the body needs extra energy.
73584.m: The basal metabolic rate is the energy needed at complete rest.

73585.q: A muesli contains 50 g carbohydrates, 10 g fat and 10 g protein. 1 g fat provides 9 kcal, and 1 g carbohydrate or protein 4 kcal each. How many kilocalories is that?
73585.e: 50 times 4 makes 200 kcal, 10 times 9 makes 90 kcal and 10 times 4 makes 40 kcal. Together that is 330 kcal.
73585.m: You work out the energy by multiplying each nutrient by its energy value.

73586.q: In which unit is energy measured in the International System of Units?
73586.e: The official unit of energy is the joule, named after James Prescott Joule. On food it usually appears as kilojoules (kJ) next to the kilocalories.

73587.q: Roughly how many kilojoules are equal to one kilocalorie?
73587.e: One kilocalorie is exactly 4.184 kilojoules, so about 4.2 kJ. 100 kcal is therefore about 420 kJ.

73588.q: What happens in the long run if you regularly eat more energy than you use?
a: Your weight definitely stays the same
73588.e: The body stores extra energy mainly as fat. The energy balance is then positive.
73588.m: If you eat more energy than you need, you gain weight.

73589.q: Which activity increases the energy you need the most?
73589.e: Exercise clearly increases the energy you use. When reading, watching TV or sleeping, you use only a little more than your basal metabolic rate.
73589.m: Exercise increases the energy you need.

73590.q: How much unsweetened drink does the Swiss food pyramid recommend for adults per day?
73590.e: About 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks a day are recommended, ideally tap water or tea. In hot weather and during sport you need more.
73590.m: Drink 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks a day.

73591.q: How many portions of vegetables and fruit does the Swiss food pyramid recommend per day?
73591.e: 5 portions a day are recommended, 3 of them vegetables and 2 fruit. One portion is about a handful.
73591.m: Eat 5 portions of vegetables and fruit every day.

73592.q: According to the Swiss dietary guidelines, roughly how much does one portion of vegetables or fruit weigh?
73592.e: One portion of vegetables or fruit is about 120 grams. That is about a handful.
73592.m: One portion of vegetables or fruit is about a handful.

73593.q: How many portions of dairy products do the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024) recommend per day?
73593.e: 2 to 3 portions of milk or dairy products a day are recommended, ideally unsweetened. One portion is, for example, 2 dl of milk or 30 g of hard cheese.
73593.m: 2 to 3 portions of dairy products a day are part of it.

73594.q: According to the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024), how often a week should you eat meat at most?
73594.e: Meat, including poultry and sausages, should be limited to 2 to 3 times a week. For protein you should vary between meat, fish, eggs, tofu and pulses.
73594.m: You should only eat meat 2 to 3 times a week.

73595.q: What is at the top of the Swiss food pyramid?
a: Sweet and salty snacks and sugary drinks
73595.e: Sweets, sugary drinks and salty snacks are right at the top. They are not necessary and should only be eaten in small amounts.
73595.m: Sweet and salty snacks belong at the top of the pyramid and only rarely on your plate.

73596.q: How many portions of grain products or potatoes do the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024) recommend per day?
73596.e: 3 portions of grain products or potatoes a day are recommended. At least half of the grain products should be wholegrain.
73596.m: Eat 3 portions of grains or potatoes a day, half of them wholegrain.

73597.q: According to the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024), how often at least should you eat pulses?
a: At least five times a day
73597.e: Pulses such as lentils, beans and chickpeas should be eaten at least once a week. They provide protein and lots of fibre.
73597.m: Pulses belong on your plate at least once a week.

73598.q: In which season are Swiss outdoor-grown strawberries in season?
73598.e: Swiss outdoor strawberries are available from about May to July. In winter, strawberries are usually imported.
73598.m: Swiss strawberries are available in early summer.

73599.q: What does it mean to shop seasonally?
a: Buying produce that is ripe in the region right now
73599.e: Seasonal produce has grown in the region at the right time of year and been harvested ripe. It has short transport routes and usually needs no heated greenhouses.
73599.m: Shopping seasonally means buying what is ripe in the region right now.

73600.q: Which vegetable is a typical autumn vegetable in Switzerland?
73600.e: Pumpkins are harvested in late summer and autumn. After that they can be stored for a long time.
73600.m: Pumpkin is a typical autumn vegetable.

73601.q: Why do imported fruits transported by plane have a poor environmental record?
a: Air transport causes a lot of CO2
73601.e: Planes use a huge amount of fuel and emit a lot of CO2. Air-freighted goods harm the climate much more than goods that come by ship or lorry.
73601.m: Air-freighted goods harm the climate a lot.

73602.q: Why can tomatoes from a heated greenhouse in winter be worse for the climate than outdoor tomatoes in summer?
a: Heating uses a lot of energy
They are harvested in the dark
73602.e: Greenhouses have to be heated in winter, often with fossil fuels. Seasonal outdoor vegetables do not need this energy.

73603.q: Which aid shows when which fruit and vegetables are in season in Switzerland?
73603.e: A seasonal calendar lists, month by month, which fruit and vegetables are available fresh from the region. It helps with seasonal shopping.
73603.m: A seasonal calendar shows what is in season.

73604.q: Which vegetables are often harvested in Switzerland in autumn and sold as stored vegetables in winter?
73604.e: Carrots, cabbage, celeriac and beetroot can be stored for months after harvest. That way there are Swiss vegetables in winter too.
73604.m: Stored vegetables such as carrots are available from Switzerland in winter too.

73605.q: Which wild herb that smells of garlic is gathered in Swiss woods in spring?
73605.e: Wild garlic grows in damp deciduous woods in spring. You must carefully tell it apart from the poisonous lily of the valley and autumn crocus.
73605.m: Wild garlic is a spring herb from the woods.

73606.q: What is the highest temperature a fridge should have?
73606.e: At no more than about 5 °C, most bacteria multiply only very slowly. A fridge thermometer helps you check.
73606.m: The fridge should be no warmer than 5 degrees.

73607.q: What temperature should a freezer reach at least?
73607.e: Frozen food is stored at -18 °C or colder. At this temperature microorganisms cannot multiply.
73607.m: Frozen food is stored at -18 degrees or colder.

73608.q: Which bacteria are often found in raw eggs and raw poultry?
73608.e: Salmonella can cause stomach and gut illnesses. Cooking food thoroughly and good kitchen hygiene protect against them.
73608.m: Raw poultry and raw eggs can contain salmonella.

73609.q: Why should you use different chopping boards for raw meat and for salad?
a: Because otherwise the meat gets dry
73609.e: Otherwise germs from the raw meat can get onto food that will not be heated any more. This is called cross-contamination.
73609.m: Raw meat and salad belong on separate boards.

73610.q: What does ‘use by’ mean on a package?
a: After that date you shouldn’t eat it
It is usually still good for a long time afterwards
It is only ripe after that date
73610.e: The use-by date is found on perishable foods such as mince. You should not eat them after this date.
73610.m: After the use-by date, food no longer belongs on your plate.

73611.q: What does ‘best before’ mean on a package?
a: Until then the maker guarantees the quality
After that it is immediately poisonous
Only after that may you eat it
It must be cooked by then
73611.e: The best-before date is the maker’s guarantee of quality. Many foods are still fine to eat after it.
73611.m: After the best-before date, food is often still good.

73612.q: What should you do with a loaf of bread that has mould in one spot?
a: Toast the bread and eat it
73612.e: The threads of the mould grow invisibly through the whole airy loaf. Many moulds make toxins, so the whole loaf should be thrown away.
73612.m: Mouldy bread is thrown away completely.

73613.q: What is the process called in which milk is briefly heated to kill germs that cause disease?
73613.e: In pasteurisation, milk is briefly heated to about 72 to 75 °C. The process is named after Louis Pasteur.
73613.m: Pasteurisation makes milk safer by heating it briefly.

73614.q: What is cooking over hot steam called, without the food lying in the water?
73614.e: When steaming, the vegetables lie in a basket above boiling water. That way fewer vitamins and minerals are lost.

73615.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
73615.e: At sea level, water boils at 100 °C. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils at a little less than 100 °C there.
73615.m: At sea level water boils at 100 degrees.

73616.q: Which cooking method starts with searing and then continues covered with a little liquid, for example for a ragout?
73616.e: When braising, meat is first seared well and then cooked until tender, covered, in a little liquid. This creates roasted flavours and a sauce.
73616.m: When braising, you sear first and then cook in liquid.

73617.q: What is it called when you dip vegetables briefly in boiling water and then cool them in ice water?
73617.e: When blanching, vegetables are dipped only briefly in rapidly boiling water and then plunged into cold water. This keeps them crunchy and colourful, for example before freezing.
73617.m: Blanching means boiling briefly and cooling straight away.

73618.q: What is cooking in hot fat called, for example for chips?
73618.e: When deep-frying, the food floats in hot fat at about 160 to 180 °C. This makes it crispy on the outside.
73618.m: Chips are deep-fried in hot fat.

73619.q: What is cooking in hot but not boiling liquid called, for example for eggs without their shells?
73619.e: When poaching, delicate foods are cooked in liquid at about 65 to 75 °C. The water should not bubble.
73619.m: When poaching, you cook in hot, not boiling, liquid.

73620.q: What forms when you sear meat hard in a hot pan?
a: A brown crust with roasted flavours
73620.e: At high heat, sugars and protein building blocks react with each other. This creates the brown crust and the typical roast flavour.
73620.m: Searing creates browning and roasted flavours.

73621.q: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker than in an ordinary pan?
a: The pressure raises the boiling temperature
73621.e: In the closed pressure cooker the pressure rises. As a result, the water only boils at about 115 to 120 °C, and the food cooks faster.
73621.m: In a pressure cooker food cooks faster thanks to the higher pressure.

73622.q: What is cooking in its own juice or with a little liquid and some fat in a covered pan called?
73622.e: When stewing, vegetables cook at about 100 °C, covered, in a little liquid or their own juice. This protects flavour and nutrients.
73622.m: Stewing is cooking with a little liquid in a covered pan.

73623.q: What is the Bio Suisse label called?
73623.e: Bio Suisse awards the ‘Bud’ label (Knospe). In Switzerland it is the best-known sign for organic food.
73623.m: The Bud is the organic label of Bio Suisse.

73624.q: What is forbidden on a farm with the Bud label?
73624.e: Bud farms may not use synthetic chemical pesticides or artificial fertiliser. Manure, grazing and crop rotation, on the other hand, are part of organic farming.
73624.m: Organic farmers do without synthetic chemical sprays.

73625.q: Which kind of transport is generally not allowed for Bud products?
73625.e: Bio Suisse generally bans air transport because it causes a great deal of CO2. Imported Bud products therefore usually come by ship, rail or lorry.
73625.m: Bud products are generally not flown in.

73626.q: What rule does Bio Suisse have for a farm that wants to produce organically?
a: The whole farm must be organic
Only the animals must be organic
Only the farm shop must be organic
73626.e: Bio Suisse follows the whole-farm principle. A farm cannot be only partly organic but must convert completely.
73626.m: With the Bud, the whole farm converts to organic.

73627.q: What is the most important aim of the Fairtrade label?
a: Fair conditions for farmers in the South
The lowest possible prices in shops
73627.e: Fairtrade wants small farmers and workers in countries of the Global South to be paid more fairly and to have better working conditions. This includes minimum prices and a premium for community projects.
73627.m: Fairtrade stands up for fair wages and prices in the Global South.

73628.q: Under which name did Fairtrade start in Switzerland?
73628.e: The Max Havelaar Foundation was founded in Switzerland in 1992 and awards the Fairtrade label. The name comes from the main character of a Dutch novel.
73628.m: In Switzerland Max Havelaar stands for Fairtrade.

73629.q: What do farmers’ organisations receive with Fairtrade in addition to the sale price?
a: A discount on seed from Europe
73629.e: As well as the minimum price, Fairtrade pays a premium. The farmers decide together whether to use it to pay for schools, wells or better machines, for example.
73629.m: The Fairtrade premium goes into community projects.

73630.q: Which fruit is an especially successful Fairtrade product in Switzerland?
73630.e: Bananas grow in tropical countries and are one of the best-selling Fairtrade products in Switzerland. Apples, cherries and plums also grow in Switzerland.
73630.m: Fairtrade bananas are very common in Switzerland.

73631.q: What does the MSC label on fish products stand for?
73631.e: MSC stands for Marine Stewardship Council. The label is given to fish from wild stocks that are not overfished.
73631.m: The MSC label stands for sustainably caught wild fish.

73632.q: Which label recognises responsible fish farming, meaning fish from aquaculture?
73632.e: The ASC label (Aquaculture Stewardship Council) is meant for farmed fish. MSC is for wild-caught fish, FSC for wood and IP-Suisse for Swiss farm products.
73632.m: ASC stands for farmed fish and MSC for wild-caught fish.

73633.q: Which environmental organisation founded the MSC in 1997 together with a food company?
73633.e: The MSC was founded in 1997 by the WWF and the company Unilever. Since 1999 it has been an independent organisation.
73633.m: The WWF helped found the MSC.

73634.q: Which label is found on wood and paper from responsible forestry?
73634.e: FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) is given to wood and paper from forests that are managed sustainably.
73634.m: The FSC label stands for sustainably used forests.

73635.q: Which animal is shown in the IP-Suisse logo?
73635.e: IP-Suisse is an association of farmers who produce in a nature-friendly and animal-friendly way. Its symbol is a ladybird.
73635.m: The ladybird is the symbol of IP-Suisse.

73636.q: What does the ecological footprint measure?
a: The area you need for your lifestyle
The number of trees in a country
73636.e: The ecological footprint works out how much biologically productive area is needed to provide food, energy and goods and to absorb waste such as CO2.
73636.m: The footprint shows how much nature we need for our lives.

73637.q: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, roughly how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived as people do in Switzerland?
73637.e: According to the FOEN, almost three Earths would be needed if everyone consumed like the Swiss population. So Switzerland uses much more than nature can replace.
73637.m: The Swiss lifestyle needs almost three Earths.

73638.q: In which unit is the ecological footprint usually given?
73638.e: The footprint is given in global hectares. One global hectare is an area with the world’s average biological productivity.
73638.m: The footprint is measured in global hectares.

73639.q: The Swiss Mathis Wackernagel helped invent a well-known measure of how much nature we use. What is it called?
73639.e: Mathis Wackernagel developed the ecological footprint in the 1990s together with William Rees. It shows how much nature a person needs for their lifestyle.
73639.m: Mathis Wackernagel is one of the inventors of the ecological footprint.

73640.q: What does Earth Overshoot Day mean?
a: From this day nature’s yearly budget is used up
On this day the Earth is at its hottest
On this day there is the most rubbish
On this day nobody may drive a car
73640.e: On Earth Overshoot Day humanity has used as many resources as the Earth can renew in the whole year. For the rest of the year it lives at the expense of the future.
73640.m: After Earth Overshoot Day we are living on credit from nature.

73641.q: Which decision is most likely to make your ecological footprint smaller?
a: Travelling by train instead of by plane
73641.e: A flight causes much more greenhouse gas per person than the same distance by train. So choosing the train uses far fewer resources.
73641.m: Taking the train instead of flying protects the environment.

73642.q: What does a country’s biocapacity show?
a: How much nature there can replace
How many organic shops there are
73642.e: Biocapacity says how many resources a country’s nature can renew. If the footprint is bigger than the biocapacity, the country is living beyond its means.
73642.m: Biocapacity shows what nature can renew each year.

73643.q: According to the FOEN, roughly how much food is lost in Switzerland every year along the whole food chain?
73643.e: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, about 2.8 million tonnes of food are lost every year because of Swiss consumption, from field to plate.
73643.m: About 2.8 million tonnes of food are lost in Switzerland every year.

73644.q: Who throws away just over a quarter of all lost food in Switzerland?
73644.e: According to a study for the FOEN, just over a quarter of food losses happen in private households. Only processing loses even more.
73644.m: A lot of food is thrown away at home too.

73645.q: Roughly how much avoidable food loss is there in Switzerland per person per year (reference year 2017)?
73645.e: For 2017, about 330 kg of avoidable food loss per person was calculated, along the whole chain from field to plate.
73645.m: In Switzerland, hundreds of kilos of food per person are lost every year.

73646.q: Which tip helps most against food waste at home?
a: Shopping with a list and a plan
73646.e: If you plan beforehand what you need, you buy less too much. That way less food goes off in the fridge.
73646.m: A shopping list helps you not to waste food.

73647.q: What is a good idea for cooked leftovers from lunch?
a: Keep them chilled and eat them later
Put them straight on the compost
73647.e: Leftovers should cool quickly and then go into the fridge, well covered. That way you can still eat them the next day or turn them into a new dish.
73647.m: Well-chilled leftovers make a new meal.

73649.q: By when does Switzerland want to halve avoidable food losses compared with 2017?
73649.e: In 2022 the Federal Council adopted an action plan against food waste. The aim is to halve avoidable losses by 2030 compared with 2017.
73649.m: Switzerland wants to halve food waste by 2030.

73650.q: Why is food waste also bad for the environment?
a: Water, land and energy were used for the food thrown away
Rubbish always makes the soil more fertile
73650.e: Growing, transporting, cooling and processing food takes many resources. If the food is thrown away, all these resources were wasted.
73650.m: With every bit of food thrown away, water and energy are lost too.

73651.q: What does the rule ‘first in, first out’ mean when putting away food supplies?
a: Put older products at the front and use them first
Throw all supplies away once a week
73651.e: If you put newly bought products at the back and move older ones to the front, you use the older ones first. That way less goes out of date and there is less rubbish.
73651.m: What was bought first is eaten first.

73652.q: What should you do once the best-before date has passed?
a: Take it back to the shop
73652.e: After the best-before date, food is often still perfectly fine. You use your eyes, nose and tongue to check whether it is still good.
73652.m: Looking, smelling and tasting helps avoid needless waste.

73653.q: Which food needs no best-before date because it keeps practically for ever?
73653.e: Table salt and solid sugar do not go off if stored dry. That is why they do not have to carry a best-before date.
73653.m: Salt and sugar keep almost for ever.

73654.q: Which food is usually still fine to eat long after its best-before date?
73654.e: Dry foods such as pasta, rice or sugar are often still good months after the best-before date. Fresh fish and mince, on the other hand, go off quickly.
73654.m: Dry supplies often keep much longer than stated.

73655.q: Where is the best place to keep dairy products after opening?
73655.e: Opened dairy products belong in the fridge, because the cold slows down the growth of bacteria. They should then be used up within a few days.
73655.m: Opened dairy products belong in the fridge.

73656.q: What does the number 30 in a washtub symbol mean?
a: Wash at no more than 30 degrees
73656.e: The number in the washtub gives the highest washing temperature in degrees Celsius. You may wash colder, but not warmer.
73656.m: The number in the washtub is the highest washing temperature.

73657.q: What does a hand in the washtub symbol mean?
73657.e: A hand in the washtub means hand wash. The garment is delicate and should not be washed in the normal machine.
73657.m: A hand in the washtub means hand wash.

73658.q: Which symbol on the care label stands for ironing?
73658.e: The iron symbol shows whether you may iron and how hot. The more dots there are in it, the hotter the iron may be.
73658.m: The iron on the label tells you about ironing.

73659.q: What does an iron with three dots mean?
73659.e: One dot stands for a low ironing temperature, three dots for a high one. Three dots are often found on cotton and linen.
73659.m: Three dots in the iron allow the hottest setting.

73660.q: What does a circle in a square stand for on the care label?
73660.e: The circle in a square is the symbol for the tumble dryer. If it is crossed out, the garment must not go in the tumble dryer.
73660.m: The circle in a square stands for the tumble dryer.

73661.q: What does a crossed-out triangle on the care label mean?
73661.e: The triangle stands for bleaching. If it is crossed out, you must not use bleach or detergent containing bleach.
73661.m: A crossed-out triangle means no bleaching.

73662.q: What does a bar under the washtub symbol mean?
73662.e: A bar under the washtub calls for milder treatment, meaning a gentle wash cycle. Two bars mean an especially gentle wash, for example for wool.
73662.m: The more bars under the tub, the gentler the wash.

73663.q: What does an empty circle on a care label mean?
a: Professional cleaning at a dry cleaner's
73663.e: The circle stands for professional textile care, for example at a dry cleaner's. Letters in the circle show which process is allowed.
73663.m: The circle on the label is for professional cleaning.

73664.q: Why do you sort laundry by colour before washing?
a: So dark colours do not run onto light ones
73664.e: New or dark clothes can release dye into the water. White or light laundry would otherwise become discoloured.
73664.m: Light and dark laundry are washed separately.

73665.q: What saves the most energy when doing the laundry?
73665.e: Most of the electricity is used to heat the water. If you wash at 30 or 40 degrees instead of 60 degrees and fill the machine well, you save a lot of energy.

73666.q: What works well against limescale stains in the bathroom?
a: An acidic product such as vinegar
73666.e: Limescale dissolves in acid. That is why vinegar or citric acid helps against limescale rings on taps and in the washbasin.
73666.m: Acidic cleaning products help against limescale.

73667.q: Which kind of cleaning product is especially good at removing grease in the kitchen?
a: An alkaline product such as soda
An acidic product such as vinegar
73667.e: Alkaline cleaners such as soda or soft soap dissolve grease and protein well. Acidic products, on the other hand, are better for limescale.
73667.m: Alkaline cleaning products help against grease.

73668.q: Why must you never mix chlorine cleaners with acidic cleaners?
a: The products then turn solid and useless
73668.e: If you mix a chlorine cleaner with acid, for example with a descaler, poisonous chlorine gas forms. It strongly irritates the airways and can be dangerous.
73668.m: Never mix chlorine cleaners and acid.

73669.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland if someone is poisoned by cleaning products?
73669.e: The number 145 belongs to Tox Info Suisse, the advice centre for poisoning. 144 is the ambulance, 117 the police and 118 the fire brigade.
73669.m: For poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on 145.

73670.q: Why should you never pour cleaning products into empty drinks bottles?
a: Someone could mistake them for a drink
The plastic would turn into glass
It is only forbidden in winter
73670.e: Children in particular can think a cleaning product in a drinks bottle is something to drink. That is why cleaning products stay in their original bottle with the hazard warning.
73670.m: Cleaning products always stay in their original bottle.

73671.q: What shape are the hazard pictograms on cleaning products?
a: A diamond with a red border
A yellow triangle with a star
73671.e: The worldwide standard hazard pictograms (GHS) are squares with a red border standing on one corner, so diamonds, with a black symbol.
73671.m: You can recognise hazard symbols by the red diamond.

73672.q: What pH value does a neutral cleaning product have?
73672.e: The pH scale goes from 0 to 14. Values below 7 are acidic, values above 7 are alkaline and exactly 7 is neutral.
73672.m: A pH value of 7 is neutral.

73673.q: What is right when measuring out cleaning products?
a: Use only as much as needed
Make as much foam as possible
73673.e: Too much cleaning product does not clean better, but it harms rivers and lakes and your wallet. The instructions on the packet help you use the right amount.
73673.m: Using the right amount is cheaper and better for the environment.

73674.q: Roughly how much heating energy do you save if you lower the room temperature by 1 degree?
73674.e: As a rule of thumb, each degree less room temperature saves about 6 per cent of heating energy. Lowering it from 22 to 20 degrees therefore saves about 12 per cent.
73674.m: Each degree less saves about six per cent of heating energy.

73675.q: What is the most energy-saving way to air a room in winter?
a: Briefly and thoroughly with windows wide open
Only opening the door at night
73675.e: When you air a room quickly with the windows wide open, the air is exchanged in a few minutes without the walls and furniture cooling down. Tilted windows, however, let heat escape for hours.
73675.m: Short, full airing is better than tilted windows.

73676.q: Why does a lid on the pan save energy?
a: The heat stays in the pan
73676.e: With a lid, less heat and steam escape. The water boils faster and you can turn the hob down sooner.
73676.m: With a lid you cook faster and more economically.

73677.q: Which lamp uses the least electricity for the same brightness?
73677.e: LED lamps turn a large part of the energy into light. Light bulbs and halogen lamps mainly produce heat and use several times as much electricity.
73677.m: LED lamps save a lot of electricity.

73678.q: What does standby mode mean for electrical devices?
a: The device is ready and still uses electricity
The device is completely cut off from the power
The device feeds electricity back into the grid
73678.e: On standby, the device waits for a command, for example from the remote control. It keeps using electricity while it does so. A power strip with a switch cuts the devices off completely.
73678.m: Devices on standby also use electricity.

73679.q: Which energy efficiency class on the energy label is the best?
73679.e: The energy label goes from A (very efficient, green) to G (not very efficient, red). A class A device uses the least energy for the same performance.
73679.m: On the energy label, A is the best class.

73680.q: Why does a fridge use more electricity if it stands right next to the oven?
a: It has to give off more heat to the outside
The oven takes electricity from it
Its door then closes less well
73680.e: A fridge releases the heat from inside it to the surroundings at the back. If it is warm there, it has to work longer. That is why you put it in a cool place with enough air.
73680.m: A fridge belongs in a cool place.

73681.q: Work it out: A family lowers the room temperature from 23 to 20 degrees. How much heating energy do they save using the rule of thumb of 6 per cent per degree?
73681.e: The temperature drops by 3 degrees. 3 times 6 per cent gives about 18 per cent less heating energy.
73681.m: Three degrees less saves about eighteen per cent of heating energy.

a: A fee you pay when buying official rubbish bags
73682.e: In most Swiss municipalities, you pay for waste disposal by buying an official rubbish bag or a fee sticker. If you produce less rubbish, you pay less.
73682.m: With the bag fee you pay for your own rubbish.

73683.q: Which principle is the bag fee based on?
73683.e: The polluter pays principle says that whoever causes the costs pays for them. People who produce a lot of rubbish pay more.
73683.m: Whoever causes rubbish pays for it.

73684.q: Where does ordinary household rubbish usually go in Switzerland?
73684.e: Since 2000, burnable waste may no longer be put in landfill in Switzerland. It is burnt in waste incineration plants, which produce electricity and district heating as they do so.
73684.m: In Switzerland, rubbish is burnt in incineration plants.

73685.q: Where do you take out-of-date medicines?
73685.e: Medicines do not belong down the drain, because their active ingredients would get into rivers and lakes. Pharmacies and chemists take them back and dispose of them properly.
73685.m: You take old medicines back to the pharmacy.

73686.q: Roughly how much municipal waste was produced per person in Switzerland in 2024?
73686.e: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, about 664 kg of municipal waste per person was produced in Switzerland and Liechtenstein in 2024. A little more than half of it was collected separately and recycled.
73686.m: In Switzerland, each person produces hundreds of kilos of waste a year.

73687.q: Roughly what percentage of PET drinks bottles were returned in Switzerland in 2024?
73687.e: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, the return rate for PET drinks bottles in 2024 was over 84 per cent. New bottles are made again from the collected PET.
73687.m: Most PET bottles in Switzerland are recycled.

73688.q: Why is it especially worthwhile to recycle aluminium cans?
a: Recycling needs only a small part of the energy of making new aluminium
Aluminium is a renewable raw material
Aluminium is only found in Switzerland
73688.e: Making new aluminium from bauxite needs an enormous amount of electricity. Melting down old aluminium saves most of this energy.
73688.m: Recycled aluminium saves a great deal of energy.

73689.q: Where do old mobile phones and other electrical devices belong?
a: Back to the shop or to a collection point
73689.e: Electrical devices contain valuable metals and harmful substances. Shops take them back for free, because an advance recycling fee was paid when they were bought.
73689.m: Shops take back electronic waste for free.

73690.q: What usually happens if you do not pay a bill on time?
a: You get a reminder, often with fees
The bank pays it for free
73690.e: Once the payment deadline has passed, the company sends a reminder and often charges extra fees. If you still do not pay, they can take legal action to collect the debt.
73690.m: Pay bills on time to avoid reminder fees.

73691.q: Work it out: Lea gets 50 francs pocket money a month and saves 15 francs of it. How much does she save in a year?
73691.e: A year has 12 months. 15 francs times 12 gives 180 francs.
73691.m: If you save a little every month, you have a nice sum by the end of the year.

73692.q: Work it out: A bike costs 600 francs. Tim saves 40 francs every month. How many months does he have to save?
73692.e: 600 francs divided by 40 francs gives 15. So Tim has to save for 15 months.
73692.m: With a savings goal you know how long you have to save.

73693.q: What does a youth allowance mean?
a: Young people manage an amount for their own spending, such as clothes, themselves
Young people get their parents' wages
The state pays all young people a wage
Young people are not allowed any spending
73693.e: With a youth allowance, young people get a fixed amount and use it to pay for agreed spending themselves, for example clothes, mobile phone or leisure. This way they learn to handle money.
73693.m: With a youth allowance, young people learn to manage their own budget.

73694.q: What is a good rule to avoid getting into debt?
a: Do not spend more than you earn
Pay bills only after a reminder
73694.e: If you only spend what you actually have, you do not get into debt. A budget helps you keep track.
73694.m: You only spend what you have.

73695.q: Work it out: Mia has 120 francs a month. She pays 30 francs for her mobile phone and 25 francs for her bus pass. How much is left for other things?
73695.e: The costs for the mobile phone and bus pass together come to 30 plus 25, so 55 francs. 120 minus 55 gives 65 francs.
73695.m: After the fixed costs you know how much money is left.

73696.q: Up to what age are young people considered minors in Switzerland?
73696.e: In Switzerland you come of age at 18. Before that, larger contracts such as a mobile phone contract need the parents' consent.
73696.m: In Switzerland you come of age at 18.

73697.q: What is the main aim of advertising?
a: To get people to buy a product
To inform neutrally about all products
73697.e: Advertising wants to attract attention and get people to buy a product or use a service. That is why it mainly shows the advantages.
73697.m: Advertising wants to make us buy.

73698.q: What does the advertising formula AIDA stand for?
73698.e: AIDA describes the stages advertising wants to achieve: attention, interest, the desire to buy and action.
73698.m: The AIDA formula describes the four stages of how advertising works.

a: Products are deliberately shown in films or videos
Products are sorted by price in the shop
Products are taken back to the warehouse
Products are handed out for free
73699.e: With product placement, a company pays for its product to appear visibly in a film, series or video. Many viewers hardly notice it.
73699.m: Advertising also hides in films and videos.

73700.q: What must influencers do if they are paid for a post?
a: Delete the post after an hour
73700.e: Paid posts must be clearly recognisable, for example with “Advertisement” or “Ad”. Hidden advertising is considered unfair.
73700.m: Paid posts must be recognisable as advertising.

73701.q: What does the Swiss Commission for Fairness in Advertising do?
a: It examines complaints about unfair advertising
73701.e: The Swiss Commission for Fairness in Advertising is the advertising industry's own watchdog. Anyone can submit a complaint about an advert to it free of charge.
73701.m: You can report unfair advertising to the Commission for Fairness.

73702.q: Why are sweets often placed right by the checkout?
a: So children and people waiting grab them on impulse
73702.e: While waiting at the checkout, customers have time, and children see the sweets at eye level. Such products are known as pester power products.
73702.m: Sweets at the checkout tempt people into impulse buys.

73703.q: What is a target group in advertising?
a: The people an advert wants to reach
The company that pays for an advert
The group that bans an advert
The customers who have already bought
73703.e: Advertising is aimed at particular people, for example young people, families or sports fans. Pictures, music and language are chosen for this group.
73703.m: Advertising is made for a particular target group.

73704.q: How can you get fewer advertising leaflets in your letterbox?
a: With a name sign in capital letters
73704.e: A “no advertising” sticker on the letterbox shows that you do not want unaddressed advertising. The distribution companies have to respect this.
73704.m: A sticker on the letterbox stops unaddressed advertising.

73705.q: How long does the legal guarantee for new products last in Switzerland?
73705.e: In Switzerland, new products have a legal guarantee of 2 years; for second-hand products it may be shortened to 1 year. However, a seller can exclude the guarantee in the contract.
73705.m: New products have a two-year legal guarantee in Switzerland.

73706.q: Is there a legal right to return online purchases in Switzerland?
73706.e: In Switzerland there is no general legal right to cancel online purchases. Many shops offer returns voluntarily; this is stated in their terms and conditions.
73706.m: When buying online, it is worth reading the terms and conditions.

73707.q: How long can you cancel a contract that was made on your doorstep?
73707.e: In Switzerland, you can cancel doorstep sales and contracts made over the phone within 14 days if the value is over 100 francs.
73707.m: You can cancel a doorstep sale within fourteen days.

73708.q: Which organisation stands up for consumers in German-speaking Switzerland?
73708.e: The Consumer Protection Foundation (SKS) was founded in 1964 and is based in Bern. In French-speaking Switzerland there is the FRC and in Ticino the ACSI.
73708.m: The Consumer Protection Foundation helps consumers.

73709.q: What must a shop in Switzerland make sure of with displayed prices?
a: The price may only be shown online
The price must be in euros
The price may be kept secret
73709.e: The price display rules require that prices for consumers are the amount actually to be paid, meaning including VAT. This way you can compare offers.

73710.q: What should you keep after buying something so you can use the guarantee?
73710.e: With the receipt you can prove when and where you bought a product. Without proof, a complaint is often difficult.
73710.m: Keep the receipt for the guarantee.

73711.q: Which SRF television programme tests products and uncovers consumer traps?
73711.e: “Kassensturz” is the consumer programme of Swiss television SRF. It tests products and reports on problems that consumers face.
73711.m: Kassensturz informs people about consumer issues.

a: An agreement in which goods are exchanged for money
73712.e: In a purchase contract, the seller promises to hand over the goods and the buyer promises to pay the price. It can also be made verbally, for example at the baker's.
73712.m: Even when shopping in a shop, you make a purchase contract.

73713.q: Which phase comes at the start of a product's life cycle?
73713.e: The life cycle begins with extracting the raw materials. Then come manufacture, transport, use and finally disposal or recycling.
73713.m: Every product begins with extracting raw materials.

73714.q: What does a life cycle assessment examine?
a: The environmental impact of a product over its whole life
73714.e: A life cycle assessment records how much energy, water and raw materials a product needs from manufacture to disposal and which emissions are produced.
73714.m: A life cycle assessment looks at a product from cradle to grave.

73715.q: What is meant by grey energy?
a: Energy for making, transporting and disposing of a product
Energy a device uses while in use
73715.e: Grey energy is hidden in a product. It was already used up before you buy it, for example when mining the raw materials and in the factory.
73715.m: Every product contains hidden grey energy.

73716.q: In which phase of its life does a smartphone cause most of its environmental impact?
73716.e: A smartphone needs many raw materials and an energy-intensive production. That is why most of the impact happens before it is even bought.
73716.m: Using a smartphone for as long as possible protects the environment.

a: A product is meant to break early on purpose
A product is built to be extra sturdy
A product is repaired for free
73717.e: With planned obsolescence, a product is supposedly built to break sooner so that you buy a new one. Whether and how often this happens is debated.
73717.m: Planned obsolescence means a deliberately short product life.

a: A meeting where people repair things together
73718.e: In a Repair Café, volunteers help repair broken things such as toasters, clothes or bikes. This makes the products last longer.
73718.m: At a Repair Café, broken things get a second life.

a: Making something new and more valuable from something old
Selling products at a higher price
73719.e: With upcycling, old materials are reused creatively, for example an old tarpaulin is turned into a bag. The product gains new value in the process.
73719.m: With upcycling, something old becomes something valuable.

73720.q: According to WWF, roughly how many litres of water are needed to produce the cotton for one T-shirt?
73720.e: Cotton needs a lot of water to grow, often from artificial irrigation. WWF gives about 2,700 litres for a single T-shirt.
73720.m: There is a lot of water in a T-shirt.

73721.q: What is an important principle of the circular economy?
a: Keeping materials in circulation for as long as possible
Throwing products away after a single use
Mining as much new material as possible
73721.e: In the circular economy, products are used for a long time, repaired and recycled at the end. This way as little waste as possible is produced.
73721.m: In the circular economy, materials stay in circulation.

73921.q: You knocked over the vase by accident. What is the honest thing to do?
73921.e: Being honest means telling the truth, even when you have made a mistake. Accidents can happen to anyone.
73921.m: Owning up to a mistake is honest.

73922.q: What is it called when someone says something untrue on purpose?
73922.e: A lie is something you say that you know is not true. You want to trick others with it.
73922.m: A lie is untrue on purpose.

73923.q: You find someone else's purse in the playground. What do you do?
73923.e: Things you find belong to someone else. If you hand them in, you help the owner get them back.

73924.q: Why is honesty important for friends?
73924.e: When friends are honest, they know they can believe each other. That is how trust grows.

73925.q: Your friend cheated in a game and you saw it. What is fair and honest?
73925.e: If you calmly mention the cheating, you stay honest and fair. Laughing or cheating yourself makes it worse.
73925.m: Calmly speak up about things that are unfair.

73926.q: What often happens when you tell one lie?
73926.e: One lie often leads to more lies so that it isn't found out. That quickly becomes tiring.
73926.m: One lie often leads to more lies.

73927.q: Which sentence is honest if you forgot your homework?
73927.e: Only the first sentence says what really happened. The other sentences are not true.
73927.m: Honest means saying what really happened.

a: A reason that isn't quite true
73928.e: With an excuse, you try to talk your way out of something. The reason you give is often not true.
73928.m: An excuse distracts from the truth.

73929.q: What makes someone a good friend?
73929.e: Good friends support each other, even when things are difficult. They are there for each other.

73930.q: Your friend is sad. What can you do?
73930.e: Asking shows that the other person matters to you. Often just listening helps.

73931.q: A new child is in the class and doesn't know anyone. What is kind?
a: Copy them to make fun of them
73931.e: New children often feel unsure. An invitation to play helps them fit in.
73931.m: New children are happy to be invited.

73932.q: Can you be friends with more than one child?
a: No, only with children from your own class
No, only with your own brothers and sisters
73932.e: You can have lots of friends. Every friendship is something special.
73932.m: You can have lots of friends.

73933.q: Your friend tells you a secret that doesn't harm anyone. What do you do?
a: Write it down and hand it out
73933.e: Keeping a secret shows that you can be trusted. Then your friend can tell you things later on too.

73934.q: Which kind of secret should you tell an adult you trust?
73934.e: Secrets where someone is afraid or being hurt can and should be told to someone you trust. That is not betrayal.

73935.q: How do you show a friend that you like them?
73935.e: Spending time together shows that someone matters to you. Playing, talking and laughing make a friendship stronger.

73936.q: Your friend made a mistake while drawing and is sad. What do you say?
73936.e: Encouraging words comfort your friend and show that you are on her side. Everyone makes mistakes.
73936.m: Good friends cheer each other up.

73937.e: A compliment is a friendly remark, for example “You've drawn that really well”. It makes others happy.

73938.q: You have three apples and your friend has none. What is kind?
73938.e: When you share, you think of others too. Then you both have something.

73939.q: You share 8 jelly sweets fairly with a friend. How many does each of you get?
73939.e: 8 divided by 2 is 4. That way you each have the same number.
73939.m: When you share fairly, everyone gets the same amount.

73940.q: Two children want the same swing. What is a good solution?
73940.e: Taking turns is a way of sharing. Everyone gets a go.

73941.q: Apart from things, what else can you share?
73941.e: You can also share time, ideas and joy with others. That costs nothing.
73941.m: You can share time and joy too.

73942.q: Can you just take something that belongs to someone else to share it?
a: Yes, if the owner is away
73942.e: Sharing something that isn't yours is only OK with permission. Otherwise you are taking something away from someone.
73942.m: Only share other people's things with permission.

73943.q: You cut a pizza into 4 equal pieces for 4 children. How many pieces does each child get?
73943.e: 4 pieces for 4 children is 1 piece per child. That is fair.
73943.m: The same number of pieces is fair.

73944.q: How do you politely ask if you can borrow something?
73944.e: Saying “please” is asking politely. Then the other person can decide for themselves.

73945.q: What do you do with a borrowed book?
73945.e: Borrowed things belong to someone else. You look after them well and give them back.

73946.q: In a race, one child starts too early. Is that fair?
a: No, everyone should start at the same time
Yes, fast people can start earlier
Yes, if they really want to win
73946.e: Starting too early gives you an unfair advantage. Everyone should start running at the same time.
73946.m: In a fair race, everyone starts at the same time.

73947.q: How does a fair winner behave?
73947.e: If you win and stay friendly, you don't hurt anyone. Laughing at others spoils the fun for everyone.

73948.q: What is fair behaviour in sport called?
73948.e: Fair play means keeping to the rules and respecting your opponent.

73949.q: How can you fairly decide who starts in a game?
73949.e: When you roll a dice, every child has the same chance. That is fair.
73949.m: Rolling a dice gives everyone the same chance.

73950.q: A child can't run because of a plaster cast. What is fair in the game?
73950.e: Being fair sometimes means being considerate. With a suitable job, the child can still join in.
73950.m: Fair is when everyone can join in.

73951.q: What is a foul in football?
73951.e: A foul is breaking the rules of the game, for example tripping someone up. There is a penalty for it.
73951.m: A foul is against the rules.

73952.q: A child has fallen over and is crying. What do you do?
73952.e: Helpful people look after others when they need help. If someone is hurt, you fetch an adult.
73952.m: Someone who falls over needs help.

73953.q: Who do you call on 144 in Switzerland after a bad accident?
73953.e: In Switzerland, 144 is the emergency number for the ambulance service, the rescue service with the ambulance.
73953.m: You reach the ambulance service on 144.

73954.q: What is the emergency number for the fire brigade in Switzerland?
73954.e: In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on 118. You call them, for example, if there is a fire.

73955.q: Which number can children in Switzerland call when they are worried?
73955.e: The number 147 from Pro Juventute is there for children and young people. Someone listens and helps there, day and night and free of charge.
73955.m: When you're worried, the number 147 helps.

73956.q: An older man is carrying heavy bags up the stairs. What is helpful?
73956.e: If you first ask whether help is wanted, you are helpful and polite. The other person can then say yes or no.
73956.m: Offer help in a friendly way.

73957.q: How can you help at home?
73957.e: Small jobs like laying the table help the whole family. Then one person doesn't have to do everything alone.

73958.q: What do you say when someone has helped you?
73958.e: Saying “thank you” shows that you value the help. That makes the helper happy.

73959.q: How does a child who is laughing and jumping feel?
73959.e: Laughing and jumping are typical signs of joy.
73959.m: Someone who laughs is often happy.

73960.q: A child has tears in their eyes and their head is hanging down. How do they probably feel?
73960.e: Tears and a hanging head often show sadness. You can ask what is wrong.

73961.q: A child is clenching their fists and has a red face. What feeling do they probably have?
73961.e: Clenched fists and a red face are often signs of anger. You can ask the child what is wrong.

73962.q: What can help when you are very angry?
73962.e: Breathing deeply calms the body. Afterwards you can say better what is bothering you.
73962.m: Deep breaths calm you down when you're angry.

73963.q: What is the feeling called when you are frightened of something?
73963.e: Fear warns us about dangers. It is good to talk to someone about it.

73964.q: You have finished painting a difficult picture. Which feeling fits?
73964.e: When you have managed something difficult, you are proud of it.
73964.m: When you've managed something, you're proud.

73965.q: What is it called when you can feel what others are feeling?
73965.e: Empathy means you sense how someone else is feeling. Then you can help better.

73966.q: What is the feeling called when you want something that someone else has?
73966.e: You feel envy when you begrudge someone something or want it yourself. Everyone has this feeling sometimes.

73967.e: All feelings are allowed, including anger and sadness. What matters is how you deal with them.

73968.q: What helps most when two children are arguing?
73968.e: When you talk to each other, you understand what is bothering the other person. That way you find a solution.

73969.q: How do you start a sentence to say what bothers you without blaming someone?
73969.e: An “I” sentence says how you feel without attacking the other person. That way the other person listens better.

73970.q: What should you do while the other person explains in an argument?
73970.e: If you listen, you find out why the other person is upset. Then it's your turn.

73971.q: What is a solution called where both sides give in a little?
73971.e: In a compromise, everyone gets some of what they want. So in the end both are fairly happy.
73971.m: In a compromise, both give in.

73972.q: Who can help if children can't sort out their argument on their own?
73972.e: Teachers or parents can help find a solution. In some schools, trained children also help as “peacemakers”.
73972.m: In a difficult argument, get help.

73973.q: What is not a good idea in an argument?
73973.e: Violence hurts and makes the argument worse. Talking, listening or taking a break help.

73974.q: Why can a short break help in an argument?
73974.e: With a bit of distance, you get calmer. Afterwards you usually talk to each other in a friendlier way.
73974.m: A break helps everyone calm down.

73975.q: What is a person called who helps two people who are arguing to sort things out?
73975.e: A mediator helps both sides listen to each other and find a solution. They don't take sides.

73976.q: Two children want to read the same book. Which solution is peaceful?
73976.e: If both read together, both get something out of it. That way there is no argument.

73977.q: You bumped into someone by accident. What do you say?
73977.e: You say sorry even if it was an accident. That way the other person knows it wasn't on purpose.

73978.q: What is part of a good apology?
73978.e: If you apologise properly, you say what you did wrong. That shows you are sorry.

73979.q: Apart from words, how can you show you are sorry?
73979.e: If, for example, you build a tower back up after knocking it over, you put the damage right. That shows you mean it.
73979.m: Putting things right shows you are sorry.

73980.q: Someone apologises to you. What can you answer?
73980.e: Accepting an apology ends the argument. Afterwards you can play together again.

73981.q: What is it called when you no longer hold a mistake against someone?
73981.e: Forgiving means letting go of being angry. That does both people good.
73981.m: Forgiving means letting go of anger.

73982.q: What would be a bad apology?
73982.e: If you blame the other person in the same sentence, you aren't really apologising. A real apology has no “but”.

73983.q: What is it called when two people become friends again after an argument?
73983.e: When two people make up, they put their argument behind them. It often starts with an apology.
73983.m: After the argument comes making up.

73984.q: When is the best time to apologise?
a: Only when the other person asks for it
73984.e: The sooner you apologise, the sooner the anger is over.

73985.e: If you let others finish speaking, you show that their opinion matters. That is respectful.
73985.m: Letting people finish speaking is respectful.

73986.q: What do people in German-speaking Switzerland often say as a greeting?
73986.e: “Grüezi” is a common, polite greeting in German-speaking Switzerland. Greeting people shows respect.

73987.q: How do you treat other people's things respectfully?
73987.e: Other people's things belong to someone else. You handle them carefully.

73988.q: How do you show respect for nature?
73988.e: If you take your rubbish with you, you protect animals and plants. That way nature stays beautiful.
73988.m: Take your rubbish home from nature.

73989.q: A child doesn't want to be hugged. What is respectful?
73989.e: Everyone can decide for themselves who may touch them. A no must be respected.

73990.q: How do you show respect for animals?
73990.e: Animals have feelings too and can feel pain. You treat them kindly and carefully.

73991.q: What is respectful on the bus?
a: Putting your feet on the seat
73991.e: Older or injured people often find it hard to stand. Offering them your seat shows respect.

73992.e: Swear words hurt others. Respectful people don't use them.

73993.q: Why are there rules at school?
a: So that everyone gets on well together
73993.e: Rules help everyone treat each other safely and fairly. Without rules there would be more arguments.

73994.q: At which colour of traffic light can you cross the road as a pedestrian?
73994.e: At green, pedestrians may cross. At red, you have to wait.

73995.q: What do you do in Switzerland before crossing a zebra crossing?
73995.e: “Wait, look, listen, walk” (in Swiss German “Warte, luege, lose, laufe”) is the Swiss road safety rule for children. You wait, look, listen and only then cross.
73995.m: Before crossing, wait, look and listen.

73996.q: How do you show in class that you want to say something?
73996.e: If you put your hand up, you wait until it's your turn. That way everyone can talk in peace.
73996.m: If you want to say something, put your hand up.

73997.q: Who can make rules together in a class?
73997.e: Many classes have a class council. There, children and the teacher discuss rules together.
73997.m: In the class council, you make rules together.

73998.q: What often happens when nobody keeps to the rules of a game?
73998.e: Rules make sure everyone knows what applies. Without them, people argue.

73999.q: What is best to wear for your safety when cycling?
73999.e: A bike helmet protects your head if you fall. That is why it is very important.
73999.m: A bike helmet protects your head.

74000.q: What are rules called that apply to everyone in a country?
74000.e: Laws are the rules of a country. In Switzerland, parliaments pass laws, and sometimes the people vote on them too.
74000.m: Laws apply to everyone in the country.

74001.q: Which rule usually applies when playing ball in the playground?
74001.e: If nobody hits anyone on purpose, nobody gets hurt. Everyone should have fun.
74001.m: When playing, never hurt anyone on purpose.

74002.q: A child speaks a different language at home. What is right?
74002.e: In Switzerland, many families speak a different language at home. Knowing several languages is a treasure.
74002.m: Knowing several languages is a treasure.

74003.q: A child uses a wheelchair. What is kind when playing?
a: Find a game they can join in
74003.e: With a bit of imagination, you can find games that everyone can join in. Nobody should be left out.

74004.q: Why is it good that people are different?
a: We can learn from each other
74004.e: Different people have different ideas and skills. So we can learn a lot from each other.

74005.q: What is it called when someone isn't allowed to join in just because they are different?
74005.e: Excluding someone hurts and is unfair. Every child wants to belong.

74006.q: A child has a different skin colour from you. What does that mean?
74006.e: Skin colour says nothing about what a person is like. All people are worth the same.
74006.m: All people are worth the same.

74007.q: What is it called when someone is picked on on purpose again and again?
74007.e: In bullying, someone is picked on or left out on purpose over a long time. Then you must tell adults.

74008.q: What is a fixed opinion about a group called, held without knowing the people?
74008.e: A prejudice is a judgement made before you know someone. It is often wrong.
74008.m: A prejudice judges before you know someone.

a: Helping a child who is being picked on
74009.e: Being brave means doing the right thing, even when it is difficult. If you help a child who is being picked on, you stand up for others.
74009.m: Brave people do the right thing.

74010.q: Is it brave to run across the road when the light is red?
a: Yes, if your friends are watching
74010.e: Putting yourself in danger for no reason is reckless, not brave. Courage needs good sense too.
74010.m: Being reckless is not being brave.

74011.q: A child is being picked on and you don't dare step in on your own. What is brave?
74011.e: Just watching doesn't help the child who is being picked on. It is brave to get help from an adult.

74012.q: You are scared of a task but you try it anyway. What are you showing?
74012.e: Courage doesn't mean not being scared. Brave people try even though they are scared.
74012.m: Courage means trying even when you are scared.

74013.q: Is it brave to say “No” when others want to do something wrong?
a: No, you should always join in
Only if you are the biggest
74013.e: It takes courage not to join in when everyone else is doing something wrong. A clear no protects you and others.
74013.m: Saying no to something wrong takes courage.

74014.q: Which sentence is brave when a child is being laughed at?
74014.e: Standing up for a child who is being laughed at shows courage. It helps the child a lot.
74014.m: Standing up for others is brave.

74015.q: Is it brave to admit a mistake?
74015.e: Admitting mistakes takes courage, because you might get into trouble. But others trust you more for it.

74016.q: What is the opposite of brave?
74016.e: A coward is someone who is too scared to do the right thing. Brave is the opposite.
74016.m: The opposite of brave is cowardly.

a: A rule for behaviour in a group
A feeling like joy or anger
74017.e: Norms are rules of behaviour that say what is expected in a community. They often come from values.
74017.m: Norms are rules that guide our behaviour in the community.

74018.q: Which example is a value and not a norm?
a: Not smacking your lips at the table
Switching off your mobile in the cinema
74018.e: A value is something that people think is important and worth striving for, such as honesty. The other examples are concrete rules of behaviour, so they are norms.
74018.m: Values say what is important, and norms say how you should behave.

74019.q: What is a norm called that is laid down by the state as a law?
74019.e: Legal norms are made by state bodies and can be enforced with penalties. Customs and traditions, on the other hand, are based on habit.
74019.m: Legal norms are laws that the state can enforce.

74020.q: What is a group's reaction called when someone keeps to or breaks a norm?
74020.e: Sanctions can be positive, such as praise, or negative, such as a telling-off or a fine. They make sure that norms are kept.
74020.m: With sanctions, a group rewards or punishes the behaviour of its members.

74021.q: Which language does the word “ethics” come from?
74021.e: “Ethics” comes from the Greek word “ethos”, which means habit, custom or character. The philosopher Aristotle established ethics as a subject of its own.
74021.m: The word ethics goes back to the Greek word ethos.

74022.q: What is the difference between morality and ethics?
74022.e: Morality means the values and rules that people actually live by. Ethics is the study that examines morality and gives reasons for it.
74022.m: Ethics is thinking about what is morally right.

74023.q: What is a situation called in which two important values are in conflict?
74023.e: In a conflict of values, you have to weigh things up, for example between honesty and sparing a friend's feelings. Both values are important, but you can't do full justice to both.
74023.m: In a conflict of values, you have to weigh up two important values.

74024.q: Which statement about norms is true?
a: They are the same everywhere in the world
They were all taken over from animals
They only apply to a single person
74024.e: Norms depend on culture and time. What used to be seen as rude can be normal today, and in other countries some rules are different.
74024.m: Norms are not fixed for ever but change with society.

74025.q: Which value is most important when you keep a promise?
74025.e: Others can rely on people who keep their promises. Reliability creates trust in friendships and in the community.
74025.m: Keeping promises shows reliability and creates trust.

a: The inner voice that judges good and bad
The ability to calculate very fast
74026.e: Conscience is the inner awareness of whether your own actions are right or wrong. It often makes itself felt as a good or bad feeling.
74026.m: Conscience is our inner voice for right and wrong.

74027.q: What is the unpleasant feeling called after you have done something wrong?
74027.e: Pangs of conscience come when you realise that you have acted against your own values. They can lead you to apologise or put something right.
74027.m: Pangs of conscience show us that we have acted against our own values.

74028.q: Which fundamental right in the Swiss Federal Constitution protects conscience?
74028.e: Article 15 of the Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and conscience. Every person may freely choose and profess their religion and their beliefs.
74028.m: Article 15 of the Federal Constitution protects freedom of religion and conscience.

74029.q: Which service can Swiss people do if they cannot do military service for reasons of conscience?
74029.e: Since 1996, anyone in Switzerland who cannot reconcile military service with their conscience can do a longer civilian service instead. It is done, for example, in hospitals, care homes or nature conservation.
74029.m: Civilian service is the alternative for those liable for military service who have a conflict of conscience.

74030.q: When does someone have a conflict of conscience?
a: When an order goes against their own conscience
When they have forgotten two pieces of homework
When they can't choose a pudding
When two friends have their birthday on the same day
74030.e: A conflict of conscience happens when you are supposed to do something that you yourself think is wrong. A famous example is Antigone from a Greek tragedy.
74030.m: A conflict of conscience happens when duty and conscience don't fit together.

74031.q: According to modern psychology, how does a person's conscience develop?
a: It is shaped by upbringing and experience
It is already complete at birth
It only appears at the age of 60
It is decided by the weather alone
74031.e: Children learn from parents, teachers and other people what is right and wrong. This forms their conscience over many years.
74031.m: Conscience grows through upbringing, role models and your own experiences.

74032.q: What does the expression “to have a clear conscience” mean?
a: You know you have done nothing wrong
You have had a thorough wash
You have saved a lot of money
74032.e: Someone with a clear or good conscience believes they have acted rightly. The opposite is a guilty conscience.
74032.m: You have a clear conscience if you are sure you have done nothing wrong.

74033.q: Which reformer is said to have declared in Worms in 1521 that his conscience was captive to the Word of God?
74033.e: At the Diet of Worms in 1521, Martin Luther refused to take back his writings. In doing so, he appealed to his conscience.
74033.m: In Worms in 1521, Martin Luther appealed to his conscience.

74034.q: What does it mean to take responsibility for an action?
74034.e: Taking responsibility means standing by what you have done and dealing with the consequences. That includes admitting mistakes.
74034.m: Responsibility means answering for the consequences of your own actions.

74035.q: From what age can a child in Switzerland be punished under juvenile criminal law?
74035.e: The Swiss Juvenile Criminal Law applies to young people from their 10th birthday. For young people, protection and education come first.
74035.m: In Switzerland, criminal responsibility begins at 10.

74036.q: At what age are you an adult in the eyes of the law in Switzerland?
74036.e: In Switzerland you are an adult at 18. This is called coming of age. Then you can, for example, vote in ballots and elections.
74036.m: In Switzerland, you come of age at 18.

74037.q: According to environmental ethics, who else are people responsible for?
74037.e: What we do today affects the lives of the people of tomorrow. That is why the philosopher Hans Jonas called for responsibility for the future of the Earth.
74037.m: We are responsible for the future of the Earth.

74038.q: What is the offence called when you don't help a person in mortal danger, even though you reasonably could?
74038.e: Article 128 of the Swiss Criminal Code punishes anyone who does not help a person in immediate mortal danger, even though they could reasonably be expected to. Often it is enough to call for help.
74038.m: Anyone who doesn't help a person in mortal danger, though they could, is committing an offence.
